opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few forces converging here.

The first is just economics. Human annotation has always been the bottleneck in computer vision. If you want bounding boxes or segmentation masks across hundreds of thousands of images, you're talking about real money and real time, often months. And the quality isn't as uniform as people assume. Annotators get tired, guidelines get interpreted differently, and you end up with a lot of label noise that you then have to go back and clean up.

The second force is that the models themselves have gotten remarkably good. With foundation models, the big vision-language models and the promptable segmentation models, you can now get zero-shot or few-shot labels that are, for many common classes, competitive with what you'd get from a human labeling pipeline. That flips the question. It used to be "how do we label this data?" Now it's more "which of these auto-generated labels can we trust, and where do we actually need a human?"

The third piece, and the one I find most interesting as a researcher, is the shift in where the value is. If labeling becomes cheap, the scarce resource isn't the label. It's understanding your data: knowing what's in your dataset, where the gaps are, where the model is confidently wrong, which edge cases matter for your application. So I see automated labeling less as replacing people and more as moving human effort upstream and downstream, toward curation, verification, and deciding what data is worth having at all.

I'd add a caveat, though. Automated labeling works best on the head of the distribution, the everyday objects these big models have seen a million times. In the long tail, specialized domains like medical imaging, certain industrial settings, or rare events in autonomous driving, you still need careful human judgment. So the realistic picture is a hybrid workflow: let the models do the bulk of the work, then put your human attention where the models are uncertain or where mistakes are costly. That's where I think the field is really heading.

r001.rationale: The response says human annotation is costly and inconsistent, with label noise requiring cleanup, but it does not clearly identify low downstream usability of human-annotated data as a cause of wasted labeling expenditure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think there are really a few forces converging at once.

The first one is just economics. If you look at where the time and money go in building a computer vision system today, the model architecture is almost a solved problem for most people. You pull something off the shelf, you fine-tune it. What's actually expensive is the data, and specifically the labeled data. Teams I talk to are spending the majority of their budget and their calendar on annotation, and a lot of that annotation is tedious, repetitive work. So there's enormous pressure to take humans out of the parts of that loop where they're not adding much judgment.

The second force is that the models themselves got good enough to help. Five or six years ago, if you tried to use a model to pre-label your data, the predictions were bad enough that correcting them took almost as long as labeling from scratch. Now, with foundation models, with things like SAM and CLIP-style embeddings, the pre-labels are often ninety-plus percent of the way there on the common cases. So the role of the human shifts from drawing boxes to reviewing and correcting, and that's a very different cost structure.

The third thing, and this is the one I think gets underappreciated, is that we've started to realize the labels we care about are not uniformly valuable. Most of the frames in a driving dataset or a retail dataset are boring. They look like a thousand other frames you already have. The value is in the tails, the rare cases, the ambiguous ones. Automation lets you handle the easy bulk cheaply, and then you can redirect your human attention to where it actually matters. That reframing, from "label everything" to "label what moves the needle," is really what makes automated labeling make sense as a strategy rather than just a shortcut.

Now, I'd add a caution. There's a seductive story that says you just let the model label the data and train on it, and I think people who've actually done it know that's where you get into trouble. The model confirms its own biases. The errors it makes are exactly the errors it won't catch. So the honest version of automated labeling isn't "no humans," it's "humans positioned where the model is uncertain or wrong," and building the tooling to find those places. That's the hard part, and I think it's where the field actually is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says annotation is costly and repetitive, and that common frames add little value compared with rare cases. It does not identify low downstream usability of human-annotated data as a cause of wasted labeling expenditure.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two forces coming together. One is the demand for labeled data. When you’re building a computer vision system, collecting images or video is often much easier than turning that material into useful training examples. And the labeling can be quite involved: you might need a box around every object, a precise boundary, or a consistent identity as an object moves through a video. Doing all of that manually becomes a real bottleneck.

The other force is that the models themselves have become useful enough to assist with that work. You can have a model propose a label and let a person correct it, rather than asking the person to start from scratch. Those corrections can then help improve the model.

So I see the shift as a change in where human effort goes. People spend less time on repetitive annotation and more time resolving ambiguity, catching mistakes, and defining what the labels should mean. The important question is how much human work you’re actually saving while maintaining the quality of the data.

r001.rationale: The response describes manual annotation as a bottleneck and model-assisted labeling as a way to save effort, but does not identify low downstream usability of human-annotated data as a source of wasted labeling expenditure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two forces coming together. One is the sheer volume of visual data. We can collect images and video much faster than we can annotate them, and with video, labeling can mean drawing an object’s boundary in frame after frame. That becomes a real bottleneck.

The other is that the models have become useful enough to participate in that process. Instead of asking a person to label everything from scratch, you can have a model propose a label and have the person correct it. Those corrections can then help improve the model.

So I see this as a shift in where human effort goes. People spend less time on repetitive annotation and more time resolving ambiguity, catching mistakes, and defining what the labels should mean. The important question is how much human effort you can save while still getting the quality you need.

r001.rationale: The response describes annotation volume as a bottleneck and models helping people label data, but it does not identify poor downstream usability of human-annotated data as a source of wasted labeling expenditure.
